04 · Read & review

The transcript

Submit all six answers to unlock the transcript. You can then listen and read together.

The following morning, Emma met Calum at a café near Waverley Station. He was in his thirties now, broad-shouldered and plainly uncomfortable with the attention. He put a folder on the table before he had even taken off his coat.

"I don't want a story about how the trust ruined my life," he said. "It didn't. I found another way to finish the course. But they told me the fees were covered, and they weren't."

Inside the folder was a copy of an award letter, a college invoice and two emails from the trust. The letter referred to support for a training course. The invoice showed an outstanding balance. In the first email, the trust said payment was being processed; in the second, written months later, it apologised for a delay and asked for patience.

"Did the college ever receive the payment?" Emma asked.

"Not from the trust. I paid the balance myself."

"Would you be willing to authorise the college to confirm that?"

"If they still have the records."

Emma photographed nothing without asking. She copied the dates, checked the names and asked Calum to send scans through a secure channel. Then she asked the question that mattered most to her investigation.

"Did you complain at the time?"

"Of course. I went to the trust's office. They said the person dealing with my file had left. I never found out who that was."

"Was it Claire Morrison?"

Calum shook his head. "I don't know. I never met her."

Outside, a tram passed the café window. Emma watched it for a moment, gathering her thoughts. It would be easy to tell herself that Claire had discovered the missing money and vanished because of it. But the documents did not yet support that conclusion. They showed a promised payment, a delay and a former student who said the money never arrived. They did not show where the money had gone, or whether anyone had acted dishonestly.

Back at the flat, she compared the two accounts. Ailsa described an award reduced without a clear explanation; Calum described fees that had not been paid at all. Their stories were not identical, and that made them more useful than a rehearsed allegation. Both had documents that might allow independent verification.

Emma drafted a list of requests. She would ask the college to confirm Calum's payment record, with his consent. She would request the trust's scholarship criteria for 2010 and 2011. She would look for minutes of trustee meetings where changes to the scheme might have been approved. And she would find out whether any independent auditor had raised questions about the difference between awards announced and payments completed.

Her cursor hovered over a blank email addressed to the foundation. Malcolm Vale's name was still on its website as chairman. She could ask him to explain the figures. She should ask him, eventually. But before offering him a chance to respond, she wanted to know exactly which facts she could prove.

Ailsa sent a photograph of the first page of her award letter that evening. Emma enlarged the image. The amount was described as a maximum, just as Ailsa had said. Beneath it, however, was a line Emma had not expected: Payment schedule to be confirmed in writing by the trust's accounts office.

There was no schedule attached. Ailsa said she had never received one.

Emma copied the sentence into her notes. She would need to verify the document and check whether a separate schedule existed. Yet it gave her a concrete question to take to the accounts office, rather than another suspicion to add to the pile.

She looked at the list of names again. Twelve people. Twelve separate histories. The brochure had made them look like a single success story. Emma now knew that at least two remembered something more complicated.

She closed the spreadsheet and opened a new page in her notebook. At the top she wrote: Who authorised the payments — and who kept the records?

Below it, almost without thinking, she wrote another name.

Fiona Kerr.
